title: Retire verify_ascending_order once dataflow graph models scalar-ALU dependencies
description:
# Goal

Delete the structural rule `verify_ascending_order` (and its supporting
test surface) once `rocm-libraries-wx9.10` lands, because the dataflow
graph + `compare_graphs` will then catch the same reordering errors
end-to-end.

DO NOT START until rocm-libraries-wx9.10 is closed.

# What the rule checks (one-line summary)

For each non-Pack key in `scheduleInfo.optSchedule`, the per-code-path
sequence of vmfma_indices must be non-decreasing — i.e. each subsequent
instruction in a category (GRIncA, GRA, LRA0, ...) must land in a vmfma
slot >= the previous one.

`OutOfOrderSequenceFailure(kind="sequence", schedule_key=<key>,
sequence=<list>, bad_value=<int>, bad_index=<int>, prev_value=<int>)`
captures the violation.

# Why this becomes safe to delete (after rocm-libraries-wx9.10)

Once `_writes()` / `_reads()` model scalar ALU registers, any reordering
of a category stream that preserves no semantically valid program order
will surface as a register-level RAW edge inversion in `compare_graphs`,
which is already wired into the production assertion path (`isValid` at
CMSValidator.py:3532-3549). The structural rule then provides no
additional coverage. See the existing test that documents this gap
explicitly: `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_comparison.py:615-712`.

# Concrete deletion list

1. `Tensile/Components/CMSValidator.py`
   - Delete function `verify_ascending_order` (lines ~3331-3373).
   - Delete class `AscendingOrderRule` (lines ~3380-3385).
   - Remove `AscendingOrderRule()` from `STRUCTURAL_RULES` (line ~3448).
   - Update the comment at lines ~3153-3157 to drop the
     `verify_ascending_order` mention. The `_last_failure` side-channel
     itself stays — `verify_scc_overlap` still uses it.
   - Update the comment at line ~3154 (rule list referenced).

2. `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_ValidateDescendingOrder.py`
   - Delete the entire file. The two tests
     (`test_non_descending_order_failure`, `test_non_descending_order_success`)
     test only the rule being deleted.

3. `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_comparison.py`
   - Delete `test_ascending_order_rule_does_catch_reversed_grinc`
     (lines 713-729). It exists solely to document why the rule
     remains necessary; once the rule is gone, the test cannot run.
   - Keep `test_reversed_grinc_chain_should_be_detected`
     (lines 674-711) — by the time we reach this bead, that test is
     green and provides the replacement coverage.
   - Update the explanatory comment block at lines 589-612 to note
     that the rule has been retired.

4. `Tensile/Tests/unit/cms_validation_base.py`
   - Update comments at lines 50 and 218 that reference
     `verify_ascending_order` as a structural-only example.

5. `Tensile/Components/ScheduleCapture.py`
   - Update the comment at lines 747-750 to drop the
     `verify_ascending_order` mention. **Do NOT delete
     `OutOfOrderSequenceFailure`** — it has a second emitter at
     CMSValidator.py:1642 (CVT0/CVT1 pair ordering, kind="cvt_pair")
     and is exercised by `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_failure_formatters.py:359`.

title: Sub-task 8: wire SCC overlap & ascending-order through typed Failure side-channel
description:
# Why this exists

The expected_message= kwarg is the only remaining string-assertion path
in cms_validation_base.validate(). Two rules feed it:

- verify_scc_overlap (CMSValidator.py:3050) - used by
  test_ValidateSCCoverlap.py (12 sites).
- verify_ascending_order (CMSValidator.py:3345) - used by
  test_ValidateDescendingOrder.py (1 site).

Removing the kwarg requires both rules to surface their failures via
the typed-Failure side-channel that the rest of the suite uses.

# Investigation findings

## Both rules already construct the typed Failure, then throw it away

- verify_scc_overlap builds SCCConflictFailure(...) at
  CMSValidator.py:3113 then calls .format(capture=None) and returns the
  string. The typed object is discarded.
- verify_ascending_order builds OutOfOrderSequenceFailure(kind=
  \"sequence\", ...) at CMSValidator.py:3373 and does the same.
- Both Failure classes are already defined in ScheduleCapture.py (lines
  583 and 623).
- ~90% of the migration is already done. The missing piece is plumbing
  the typed object back to test infrastructure.

## Why these tests don't already use expected_failure=

Both tests set needs_timeline = False and override validation_function
to call the rule directly. The existing typed-Failure side-channel in
cms_validation_base.validate() looks at timeline._last_failure - but
there is no Timeline for structural rules. So the failure has nowhere
to live between the rule returning and the test asserting.

## Rocisa instructions in the SCC-protected chain

incrementSrd (KernelWriterAssembly.py:8906-8942) emits the protected
sequence. With Use64bShadowLimit=1, four SCC-coupled groups
corresponding to intervalSize = [3,2,2,2] in verify_scc_overlap:

- Group 1 (size 3): SCmpEQU32, SCSelectB32, SCSelectB32 - cmp sets SCC;
  both selects read it
- Group 2 (size 2): SAddU32, SAddCU32 - add sets carry; addc reads it
- Group 3 (size 2): SSubU32, SSubBU32 - sub sets borrow; subb reads it
- Group 4 (size 2): SCmpEQU32, SCSelectB32 - cmp sets SCC; select reads it

With Use64bShadowLimit=0, intervalSize = [3,2,1] - group 3 collapses to
a lone SSubU32 (the upstream SAddU32/SAddCU32 carry pair stays; the
borrow chain is dropped along with the shadow-limit subtract).

Every one of these instructions has dst / src0 / src1 rocisa register
fields. They are reachable from the validator at runtime via
context.id_map[GRIncName] (the validator already has full access to the
rocisa list - verify_correct_number_of_instructions at
CMSValidator.py:3339 reads context.id_map[name] directly).

However SCC itself is not a register field on these instructions. SCC
is an implicit GPU flag, conveyed only by which opcode an instruction
is. So enriching the Failure with rocisa register identifiers would
tell a reader which sgprs are being added/subtracted/compared - not
anything new about the SCC dependency itself, which is determined by
class name. Useful for richer diagnostics, but not required for the
typed-Failure migration.

# Brainstormed approaches

## Approach A - ValidationContext._last_failure side-channel (recommended)

- Add _last_failure: Optional[Failure] = None to ValidationContext
  dataclass.
- In verify_scc_overlap (the inner verifyIndices helper) and
  verify_ascending_order, set context._last_failure = failure before
  return (False, failure.format(capture=None)).
- In cms_validation_base.validate(), after rule returns False, fall
  back to ctx._last_failure when timeline._last_failure is unavailable.
- Delete expected_message kwarg; convert the 13 test sites to
  expected_failure=Cls, expected_fields={...}.
- Smallest delta. Mirrors the existing _last_failure pattern on
  Timeline. No rule contract change; the (bool, str) return shape
  stays.
- Risk: side-channel state on a shared mutable context can leak across
  rules in isValid if not reset. Mitigated by clearing _last_failure to
  None at the top of each rule iteration in isValid.

## Approach B - change rule return type to (bool, str | Failure)

- Rules return either (False, str) (legacy escape hatch) or (False,
  failure_object).
- isValid does message = result[1].format(capture=None) if
  isinstance(result[1], Failure) else result[1].
- Test infrastructure introspects the second tuple element directly.
- Cleaner contract; eliminates the side-channel.
- Risk: every StructuralRule.run caller (currently 2 - isValid loop +
  the test override) has to handle the union. More invasive.

## Approach C - three-tuple (bool, str, Failure | None)

- Rules return (True, \"\", None) or (False, message, failure).
- Avoids the union-type ambiguity of B but bloats every return
  statement.
- No clear win over A.

## Approach D - adapter Timeline for structural rules

- Build a minimal Timeline solely so _last_failure has somewhere to
  live.
- Most complex; fights the existing \"structural rules don't need a
  Timeline\" design and would require synthesizing GraphNodes for
  instructions that have no MFMA-index meaning.

## Optional enrichment (orthogonal to all four approaches)

SCCConflictFailure could grow rocisa-instruction references - e.g.,
interval_producer_inst (the SCmpEQU32 / SAddU32 that sets SCC) and
conflicting_inst (the rogue scalar op clobbering it) - by indexing into
context.id_map[grinc_name] and context.id_map[conflicting_name]. Tests
run with mock id_maps where every GRInc entry is a duplicate
SCmpEQU32, so the enrichment is meaningful only against real captures.
Defer until there's a diagnostics consumer that needs it.

# Recommended implementation (Approach A, ~120 lines)

1. ValidationContext: add _last_failure: Optional[Failure] = None
   field + reset hook.
2. verify_scc_overlap / verifyIndices: set context._last_failure =
   failure before formatting.
3. verify_ascending_order: same.
4. cms_validation_base.validate(): read ctx._last_failure as fallback
   to timeline._last_failure; delete expected_message kwarg + the
   mutual-exclusion assertion.
5. test_ValidateSCCoverlap.py: convert 12 sites to typed assertions
   (helper: assert_scc_conflict(failure, *, conflicting_name,
   grinc_name, conflicting_index, interval_start, interval_end)).
6. test_ValidateDescendingOrder.py: convert 1 site to typed assertion
   (helper: assert_out_of_order_sequence(failure, *, schedule_key,
   sequence, bad_value, bad_index, prev_value)).
7. isValid loop: clear context._last_failure = None between rules to
   prevent cross-rule leakage.

# Verification

pytest Tensile/Tests/unit/test_ValidateSCCoverlap.py
Tensile/Tests/unit/test_ValidateDescendingOrder.py should pass; full
suite tox -e unit should also stay green.

title: Implement topology-equivalent comparison in compare_graphs (supersedes symbolic-register canonicalization)
description:
> **NOTE (2026-05-06): Working assumption flipped.** The registered gfx1151 CMS schedules (`_get_schedule_*_gfx1151`) cannot be trusted as correct. Any default-vs-CMS capture divergence is evidence the CMS schedule is wrong, not a signal to loosen the validator or extend coverage to bad schedules. The schedule corpus has since been removed entirely (commits on `validator_long_term_plans` revert 284c1fa); references to gfx1151 in this bead should be read as historical context.

---

Two related concerns about string-based registers, both currently
documented as known limitations. Defer until a kernel actually
triggers them.

# 7a. Same logical register with different identifiers across captures

Pinned in test_dataflow_graph_comparison.py::
test_symbolic_and_numeric_for_same_logical_reg_unchanged as a
documented limitation. If two captures construct the SAME physical
register with DIFFERENT identifiers (one symbolic, one numeric for
the same vgpr), render-strings differ and identities differ. Doesn't
arise in current code paths because both captures consume the same
writer state, but a future scheduler that constructs registers
differently could trigger it.

Fix path: name-resolution table approach - build {symbolic_name ->
numeric_idx} from writer state and canonicalize all register
references before identity construction.

# 7b. Topology equivalence - different register names, same dependency structure

Two graphs with the SAME topology (same instructions, same
producer-consumer pairs, same edge kinds) but DIFFERENT register
strings labeling those edges should be considered equivalent. The
current render-string identity treats them as different because the
register name is part of the rendered text.

Three approaches considered:

- Interpretation A - emit-order canonical IDs + drop register from
  edge equality key. Simple. Risk: loses sensitivity to actual
  register changes.
- Interpretation B - full graph isomorphism with register-name
  renaming. Most pure; more code; slower.
- Interpretation C - per-graph register canonicalization with
  placeholders. Same effective behavior as A.

Open questions to answer post-migration:

- Is the topology-equivalence requirement defensive (\"future-proof\")
  or does an actual scenario exist where the schedulers differ in
  register names but match in structure?
- How should the comparison handle \"topology matches but registers
  genuinely differ\"? Treat as equal? Treat as equal with warning?
  Treat as equal only when registers are symbolic?
- Should the canonical ordering be per-class-per-body or
  per-category-per-body?
- For diagnostic Failures whose producer/consumer carry register info,
  which graph's register name should the formatter prefer when they
  differ?

# Status

Both 7a and 7b are documented limitations rather than active failures.
Sub-task 3 (already shipped) unblocked this by making compare_graphs
authoritative. Fix only when a kernel actually triggers them.

## Implementation directives

- **Must be launched with an Opus 4.7 agent.** When dispatching this bead's work to a subagent, set `model: "opus"` explicitly. Do not let the dispatch fall through to default model selection — the bead is non-trivial enough to need Opus 4.7 specifically.
- **Do not write fallback paths or backwards-compatibility shims.** This codebase is in a clean-implementation effort. Defensive `getattr`, optional-flag-with-old-default, "leave the old API and add a parallel new one" patterns make the code worse and accumulate kludge. Take the change all the way: replace the old shape, fix the call sites, delete the dead path. If a refactor would require updating N test fixtures to opt in to the new shape, update all N — that is correct work, not extra work.

comments.text:
# wx9.3 Research Report: Comparing Kernel Dataflow Graphs Modulo Register Renaming

> **Provenance disclosure.** WebSearch and WebFetch were both returning 400 errors
> ("claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 deployment not found") for the entire duration of this
> task, so I could not perform live web research. This report is written from training
> knowledge of the literature and tools listed. URLs are accurate to my knowledge but
> have not been re-verified in this session — treat them as starting points, not as
> ground truth, and spot-check before quoting them externally.

---

## TL;DR recommendation

Implement **two-pass canonicalization, not isomorphism search**. Your two graphs are stipulated
to have identical topology — so you do not need general graph isomorphism. You need a
deterministic *canonical relabeling* of registers that is a function of position in the
dataflow graph, applied to both sides, after which the existing string-hash comparison
"just works." This is exactly what compilers call **value numbering** / **SSA renaming to a
canonical form**. The right algorithm is a **1-WL (color refinement) pass keyed on the SSA
def-site**, which is O((V+E) log V) and handles every realistic case you will see in a
GEMM kernel. Reserve nauty/bliss-style isomorphism only as a fallback for the
"topology-equivalent but not order-equivalent" mode, behind your flag.

The symbolic-vs-numeric naming sub-problem (7a) is solved at the **frontend** of graph
construction, not in the comparator: resolve every name through a single
`SymbolMap` to a canonical token before any node is hashed. Do not let the comparator
see two spellings of the same physical register.

---

## 1. Canonical algorithms for this problem class

### 1.1 Color refinement / 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL)

**Core idea.** Initialize every node's color to its label (opcode + operand kinds, *not*
register names). Repeatedly refresh each node's color to a hash of `(own color,
multiset of (edge-label, neighbor color))`. Iterate to fixpoint. After fixpoint, two
nodes with the same color are indistinguishable by any local-structural test of this
power. To get a *canonical labeling* of registers, replace the register name on each
edge with a tuple `(producer-color, consumer-color, ordinal)` where `ordinal` breaks
ties among parallel edges in a deterministic order (e.g. by sorted consumer color).

**Cost.** O((V+E) log V) using the Cardon-Crochemore / Paige-Tarjan partition
refinement formulation. In practice tens of microseconds for a 1000-node graph in
Python with `dict`-of-tuples coloring.

**Invariants required.** Edges must be deterministically iterable. Node labels must be
canonicalized first (opcode + literal operands, *not* renamings).

**When it works.** Whenever you only need to distinguish nodes up to local structural
equivalence, which is *exactly* your case: the two graphs differ only in register
names, and a register name in SSA dataflow is determined up to renaming by
`(def-site identity, use-site identities)` — which is what 1-WL recovers.

**When it fails.** 1-WL famously fails to distinguish certain regular graphs (e.g.
two non-isomorphic strongly regular graphs with the same parameters). This is
irrelevant to your problem: dataflow graphs of straight-line code are extremely
asymmetric — every instruction has a distinct opcode/operand position, and roots
(kernel argument loads) and sinks (stores, output writes) are pinned. You will
essentially never hit a refinement collision on real kernels. If you ever do, it
falls into the "two registers genuinely interchangeable in this kernel" bucket,
which is exactly the equivalence you want anyway.

### 1.2 Backtracking canonical labeling: nauty / bliss / Traces

**Core idea.** Run color refinement, then descend an "individualization-refinement"
search tree: pick a node from the smallest non-singleton cell, individualize it
(give it a unique color), refine again, recurse. Maintain the lex-smallest labeling
seen and prune branches that cannot beat it. The result is a canonical adjacency
matrix that is invariant under isomorphism.

**Cost.** Worst case super-polynomial; in practice fast on graphs with few
automorphisms. nauty/bliss handle 10^4–10^5 nodes routinely on combinatorial graphs.

**Invariants required.** Vertex coloring must be a proper invariant (i.e. iso-stable).

**When it works.** General graph isomorphism / canonical-form. Use this if you ever
need to compare two kernels that have **different scheduling order** (not just
different register names) and you cannot pin nodes by execution position.

**When it doesn't.** Overkill when 1-WL already distinguishes everything, which it
will for your inputs. The cost of integrating a C library (`pynauty` is a Python
binding) is not justified for the renaming-only case.

### 1.3 Value numbering / SSA renaming as canonicalization

**Core idea.** This is the classic compiler trick. Walk instructions in dataflow
order; assign each definition a value number that is a hash of `(opcode, ordered
value-numbers of operands)`. Two definitions with the same value number compute
the same value. To compare two SSA programs modulo renaming, compute value numbers
on both sides and compare value-number-streams instead of register-name-streams.

**Cost.** O(V+E) single pass after a topological sort.

**Invariants required.** SSA form (each register defined exactly once) and a
topological order. Both are properties of straight-line dataflow graphs.

**When it works.** Perfectly for your "identical topology, different names" case.
This is essentially 1-WL specialized to DAGs and is the textbook approach for
"is this CSE-equivalent transformation correct."

**When it doesn't.** When opcodes have semantic identities (e.g. `add` is
commutative, so `add r1, r2` and `add r2, r1` should hash equal). You handle this
by sorting operands of commutative opcodes before hashing — a known rocBLAS/Tensile
issue since GFX assembly has commutative `v_add_*` and `v_mul_*` family
instructions, plus FMA where only two of the three operands commute.

### 1.4 SMT / symbolic-execution equivalence (Alive2 / translation validation)

**Core idea.** Encode each kernel as an SMT formula over abstract values
(`f1(inputs) = vector of outputs`), then ask the solver `forall inputs.
f1(inputs) == f2(inputs)`. Register names disappear because they are just
intermediate variables that get existentially-eliminated.

**Cost.** Solver time, often seconds-to-minutes; exponential in the worst case.
Numerical types (float, especially fp8/bf16) blow up the encoding.

**Invariants required.** Precise semantics for every opcode. For VALU/MFMA/DS
instructions on AMD GCN, this is a major undertaking — there is no published
SMT-LIB-bit-precise model of MFMA.

**When it works.** When you can afford the modeling cost and you actually need
*semantic* equivalence (not just structural). Alive2 does this for LLVM IR; CompCert
does it as machine-checked proof for RTL→Mach.

**When it doesn't.** Now. You don't have semantics for every GFX opcode and you
don't need them — you stipulate the two graphs are **already the same up to
register renaming**, which is a much weaker check than full semantic equivalence.
Don't pay for what you don't need.

### 1.5 Translation validation (Necula, Pnueli/Siegel/Singerman)

**Core idea.** For each compilation, emit a *witness* mapping source variables
to target variables (a simulation relation). The validator only checks the
witness, not the optimization. Necula's PLDI'00 paper and the
Pnueli/Siegel/Singerman TACAS'98 paper are the foundational references.

**Relevance to you.** You don't have a witness — the scheduler doesn't emit a
register correspondence. But this is **exactly** the framework you would adopt if
you ever wanted to validate SIA0 → SIA3 across genuinely different schedules.
The current approach (compute the correspondence post-hoc by 1-WL on the dataflow
graph) is essentially "infer the simulation relation from structure."

### 1.6 Peephole verifiers: Souper, Alive

Souper extracts an SSA "candidate optimization" (LHS DAG → RHS expression),
canonicalizes both sides by **renaming all variables to `%0, %1, ...` in a
deterministic dataflow walk**, and then queries the SMT solver. The
canonicalization step alone is what you want — it makes structurally-equivalent
candidates *string-equal*, which lets Souper deduplicate its candidate cache by a
hash. This is the cheapest, most pragmatic version of what we are recommending.

---

## 2. How real projects solve it

(URLs from memory; verify before citing externally.)

- **LLVM `MachineCSE` / `EarlyCSE`** — value-numbering on MachineInstrs. Each
  MachineInstr gets a hash of (opcode, hashed operands), with virtual register
  *defs* stripped so renaming doesn't perturb the hash and *uses* substituted with
  the value-number of their producer. This is item 1.3 above, in production.
  See `llvm/lib/CodeGen/MachineCSE.cpp`. <https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/llvm/lib/CodeGen/MachineCSE.cpp>

- **LLVM `MachineVerifier`** — checks SSA invariants and register-class
  consistency, not equivalence. Mentioned because people reach for it and it is
  the wrong tool. <https://llvm.org/docs/MIRLangRef.html>

- **GCC `-fcompare-debug`** — compiles twice (once with, once without debug
  info), strips debug, and checks the assembly streams are byte-identical. The
  *deliberate design choice* is that GCC normalizes register allocation enough
  that byte equality is achievable. The lesson for you: if you can make the
  scheduler emit registers in a deterministic *position-derived* order, you don't
  need any clever comparator — `diff` works. This is the cleanest long-term fix.
  <https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gccint/Compare_002ddebug.html>

- **Souper** — canonicalizes SSA by renumbering all internal vars during DFG
  walk, then SMT-checks. Key insight: *canonicalize first, hash second; the
  expensive checker is a fallback, not the primary equality test.*
  <https://github.com/google/souper>

- **Alive2** — translation validator for LLVM IR. Source and target have
  independent SSA name spaces; Alive2 binds them via positional argument
  matching at function entry, then refinement-checks the rest symbolically.
  <https://github.com/AliveToolkit/alive2>, paper: Lopes et al., PLDI'21,
  "Alive2: Bounded Translation Validation for LLVM."

- **CompCert** — register allocation (Coloring → Allocation) is verified by a
  Coq proof that the *interference graph + coloring* preserves the source RTL
  semantics. The proof is *witness-based* (the coloring is the witness). See
  Leroy, JAR'09, "A Formally Verified Compiler Back-end."
  <https://compcert.org/>

- **Equality saturation / egg / Peggy** — represents all known equivalents as
  an e-graph, where each e-class is a canonical equivalence class of values.
  Register names are e-class IDs. Two terms are equal iff they share an e-class.
  Excellent if you ever need to grow the equivalence to algebraic identities.
  egg paper: Willsey et al., POPL'21. <https://egraphs-good.github.io/>

- **STOKE** (Stanford superoptimizer for x86-64) — equivalence-checks two
  basic blocks under register renaming by symbolic execution and a per-register
  permutation match. Relevant because it operates on *machine* code, not IR,
  same regime as you. <https://github.com/StanfordPL/stoke>

- **BinDiff / Diaphora** — binary function matching across compilations.
  Multi-stage matching: hash on call-graph signature, then on CFG fingerprint
  (per-BB instruction-class histograms, *not* register names), then on
  Weisfeiler-Lehman-style label refinement. The two-tier "cheap structural hash
  → expensive iso check" pattern is the right architecture for your validator
  too. <https://www.zynamics.com/bindiff.html>

- **Triton compiler** — lowers TritonGPU IR through MLIR; uses MLIR's
  `OperationEquivalence` which hashes on opcode+operand-position, ignoring SSA
  value names. Same idea as MachineCSE but at MLIR level.
  <https://mlir.llvm.org/doxygen/classmlir_1_1OperationEquivalence.html>

- **AMD ROCm / Tensile** — no public equivalence checker that I'm aware of;
  this validator is filling a real gap.

---

## 3. Recommendation for your specific case

### 3.1 The algorithm

Use **SSA value numbering as canonical relabeling**, run during graph
construction or as a single pass over the existing graph:

1. **Topo-sort** the dataflow graph (you already have it; it's the instruction
   order in the kernel).
2. For each node in order, compute `vn(node) = hash(opcode_canonical,
   sorted_or_ordered_tuple_of(vn(operand) for operand in operands))`. For
   commutative opcodes, sort operand value-numbers; for non-commutative, keep
   positional order.
3. For each *register definition* by node `n`, assign canonical name
   `"r" + base32(vn(n))` (or just the integer `vn(n)`).
4. Rewrite every edge in the graph to use these canonical names instead of
   `v34`/`v52`.
5. Compare the two graphs with your existing string-hash comparator. They will
   match.

This is O(V+E), single pass, no library dependencies, no SMT solver.

For the "topology-equivalent but different schedule order" mode (your flag),
fall back to **1-WL color refinement** over the graph instead of step 1's
topo-walk. Same hashing rule; iterate to fixpoint instead of single-pass. Still
O((V+E) log V).

Reserve **bliss/nauty** for a possible future "two functionally-equivalent
kernels with different topology" mode (SIA0 vs SIA3 with reorderings that change
the DAG, e.g. fused vs unfused). Don't build it now.

### 3.2 Data structure changes

- Introduce a `CanonicalForm` object that wraps a graph and exposes
  `node.canonical_id` and `edge.canonical_register`. Compute it once,
  cache it on the graph.
- Your existing canonical string is built from `node.id + edge.label`. Change
  *only* the edge.label source from `register_name` to
  `edge.canonical_register`. The hashing/comparison logic upstream stays
  identical.
- Build canonical form **post-hoc** rather than during graph build. This keeps
  the graph constructor honest about what the kernel actually said and lets the
  validator print both the original and canonical names in diff output, which
  is essential for debugging when the comparator says "different" and you need
  to find the offending instruction.

### 3.3 Pitfalls

- **Commutative opcodes.** `v_add_f32 v1, v2, v3` ≡ `v_add_f32 v1, v3, v2`.
  Sort operand value-numbers before hashing for commutative ops. Maintain an
  explicit `COMMUTATIVE_OPCODES` set; AMD GCN ISA manuals enumerate them, and
  you must include FMA's two-of-three commutativity carefully.
- **Multi-def instructions.** Some opcodes (e.g. carry-out adds, MFMA producing
  multiple AGPRs) define more than one register. Value-number each def
  independently as `vn(node, def_index)`.
- **Memory operations.** Loads/stores have a register operand that is an
  *address* and a register operand that is *data*. The address producer is part
  of the dataflow; the memory itself is a side-effect. Model loads as
  `vn = hash(opcode, vn(addr), memory_version)` where `memory_version`
  increments at every store. Otherwise two loads from the same address get the
  same value-number even when a store between them invalidated the value.
- **Predicate / EXEC / SCC / VCC.** GCN has implicit register dependencies on
  SCC (scalar carry/condition), VCC (vector carry/condition), EXEC (execution
  mask), and M0. Treat them as first-class registers in the dataflow graph or
  the canonicalization will silently miss WAW hazards through them. This is the
  single most common bug class for AMD GPU dataflow analyzers.
- **Immediates.** Bake immediates into the opcode label, never into the operand
  list as if they were register references. Otherwise an immediate `0` collides
  with the value-number of any register that happens to be `0`.
- **Register pairs / wide registers.** `v[4:5]` vs `v[6:7]` — canonicalize the
  pair by the value-number of the *def*, then have a per-pair-element hash so
  consumers reading only the low half get a distinct value-number from
  consumers reading the full pair.
- **Phi-like joins** at loop headers (if your graph is for a loop body):
  introduce an explicit phi node so cycles in the dataflow are broken
  deterministically. Without this, value-numbering doesn't terminate.

### 3.4 Symbolic-vs-numeric naming (sub-problem 7a)

Solve at the **graph build frontend**, not in the comparator:

- Maintain a single `SymbolMap` that resolves *every* register reference,
  symbolic (`vgpr_acc_0`) or numeric (`v34`), to a unique
  `PhysicalRegister` object.
- The mapping is rebuilt per-kernel from rocisa's symbol table at parse time.
- Every node and every edge stores `PhysicalRegister` references, not strings.
- Stringification (for the canonical hash) goes through
  `PhysicalRegister.canonical_name()` which returns one and only one spelling.

Once you do this, the canonical-form pass in §3.1 sees only one name per
physical register, and the symbolic-vs-numeric divergence cannot leak into the
comparator. Build a regression test where the same kernel is parsed twice with
the symbol table forcibly inverted between symbolic and numeric — they must
hash identically.

### 3.5 Edge cases that will trip you

- **Dead defs.** Instructions whose result is never used (debug, masked-out
  lanes, optimization slack). Their value-number contributes nothing to any
  consumer, so a missing dead def on one side and a present one on the other
  will diff. Decide deliberately: either prune dead defs as a normalization
  step, or treat their absence as a real difference.
- **Renamable vs reserved registers.** SGPRs holding kernel arguments and
  certain ABI-fixed registers (s[0:1] kernarg pointer, etc.) must *not* be
  renamed by the canonicalizer — they are pinned by ABI. Mark them
  non-renamable in `PhysicalRegister` and have the canonicalizer pass them
  through.
- **MFMA accumulator chains.** A long chain of MFMAs writes the same AGPR
  tile; the value-number of each MFMA in the chain is a function of the
  previous one. Chain length must match exactly; one extra MFMA on either side
  shifts every downstream value-number. This is desirable behavior — that *is*
  a real difference — but expect noisy diffs when it fires, and surface the
  "first divergent value-number" position to make triage tractable.
- **Scheduler-inserted `s_waitcnt` and `s_nop`** — these have no def but they
  do have ordering effects. Model them as nodes with empty value-numbers or
  exclude them from canonicalization (then compare them positionally as a
  separate stream).
- **Unique-ifying hash collisions.** Use at least 64-bit value-numbers; a
  32-bit hash will collide on real kernels (1000 nodes, birthday bound ≈ 50%
  collision risk near 65k value-numbers but cumulative across regression runs
  the risk grows). Python's built-in `hash` is not stable across runs unless
  you set `PYTHONHASHSEED`; use `hashlib.blake2b(digest_size=8)` or stable
  64-bit FNV.

---

## 4. References (prioritized, top 8)

1. **Cooper, Simpson, Vick, "Operator Strength Reduction" / "Value Numbering"
   (TR94-242, Rice).** The foundational SSA value-numbering paper. Read this
   first; it's the algorithm in §3.1 in 12 pages.
   <https://www.cs.rice.edu/~keith/EMBED/dom.pdf> (or the Rice TR series)

2. **Lopes, Menendez, Nagarakatte, Regehr, "Alive2: Bounded Translation
   Validation for LLVM," PLDI 2021.** The state of the art for IR-level
   equivalence; explains why register naming is encoded existentially.
   <https://web.ist.utl.pt/nuno.lopes/pubs/alive2-pldi21.pdf>

3. **Necula, "Translation Validation for an Optimizing Compiler," PLDI 2000.**
   The classical translation-validation paper; the witness-based framing your
   long-term SIA0/SIA3 effort will end up in.
   <https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~necula/Papers/tv00.pdf>

4. **Pnueli, Siegel, Singerman, "Translation Validation," TACAS 1998.** The
   other foundational TV paper, predating Necula.

5. **Junttila, Kaski, "Engineering an Efficient Canonical Labeling Tool for
   Large and Sparse Graphs" (bliss).** The most accessible engineering
   description of nauty-class algorithms. Read if you ever build the
   topology-different mode.
   <https://users.aalto.fi/~tjunttil/bliss/>

6. **Willsey et al., "egg: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation," POPL
   2021.** If you ever want to grow equivalence beyond renaming (e.g. algebraic
   reassociation), read this.
   <https://egraphs-good.github.io/>

7. **LLVM `MachineCSE.cpp` source.** Production-grade SSA value numbering on
   machine instructions, including the commutative-operand and multi-def
   handling you need. Read the `isPhysDefTriviallyDead` / `ProcessBlock`
   functions.
   <https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/llvm/lib/CodeGen/MachineCSE.cpp>

8. **GCC `-fcompare-debug` documentation and the Bugzilla history that
   motivated it.** The clearest case study of "make the compiler deterministic
   so byte-diff works" as an alternative to building a clever comparator. The
   right long-term answer if your scheduler can be made deterministic.
   <https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gccint/Compare_002ddebug.html>

---

## Closing opinion

You are over-thinking this if you reach for graph isomorphism. The *real*
problem is that you let register names — which are arbitrary labels assigned
downstream of any semantic decision — into the canonical form upstream of the
comparator. Strip them out by replacing every register name with a value-number
derived from the dataflow position of its definition; keep the topology
otherwise unchanged; let your existing comparator do its existing job. This is
~150 lines of Python, no new dependencies, O(V+E), and matches what every
production compiler does for the same problem at IR level.

The flag for "topology-equivalent but reordered" is the only place 1-WL
iteration earns its keep, and it is a 20-line extension to the same code path.

Save SMT, nauty, and equality saturation for the day you actually need to
compare two kernels that compute the same answer with genuinely different
algebra. That day is not today, and when it comes, the right tool will be
Alive2-shaped, not nauty-shaped.

comments.text:
## Reframe (2026-05-08): topology-equivalent comparison, not name resolution

The original 7a/7b framing assumed the fix was to **canonicalize register names** so identity-based comparison could match across graphs (and within one graph for mixed symbolic+numeric forms). That framing led to the c70 `allocation_table` speculation and the d0xd follow-up epic — both of which were predicated on building a name-resolution layer.

After review, the right direction is **topology-equivalent comparison**: compare graphs structurally (matched by node role and position, edges keyed by role-pair + edge kind), with register names treated as *internal* identity within one graph (used by the graph builder to wire edges) rather than *cross-graph* identity (used by compare_graphs to match nodes).

This collapses both sub-tasks:
- **7a** (intra-graph mixed identifiers): the graph builder needs *some* canonicalization to know two operand references within one graph are the same register, but it does NOT need to be allocation-table-based. Cheap local rules work — rename in first-write order, hash the rocisa container, or similar.
- **7b** (cross-graph topology equivalence): solved directly. Register names never enter the comparison signature; (src_role, sink_role, edge_kind, byte_offset) is the edge key.

## Why this reframe

- Neither 7a nor 7b is firing today (per this bead's own status: 'documented limitations rather than active failures').
- The c70 `allocation_table` parameter was removed because no caller passed it and no test exercised it.
- d0xd Phase 1 (commit 6b3b68eacd) confirmed: no current code path needs the mechanism; wx9.3 is the only named consumer; wx9.3 itself is deferred until triggered.
- The symbolic→numeric direction also requires solving asymmetric per-thread global vgpr state and mid-build sgpr mutability — substantial complexity for a problem that may never need solving.
- Topology-equivalent comparison sidesteps both register-identity problems for the cross-graph case AND has the side benefit of catching genuine topology-only divergences that name-based comparison would also catch.

## Approaches in scope (per the original 7b options, with the prior preference flipped)

- **Interpretation A** (emit-order canonical IDs + drop register from edge equality key): now preferred.
- **Interpretation B** (full graph isomorphism with register-name renaming): higher cost, equivalent power.
- **Interpretation C** (per-graph register canonicalization with placeholders): same effective behavior as A; pick whichever is cleaner to implement.

## d0xd disposition

d0xd is being closed as obsolete (the symbolic→numeric direction is no longer the chosen approach). Its Phase 1 memo (`Tensile/Components/SYMBOLIC_REGISTER_RESOLUTION_PHASE1.md`) stays as historical context for why this direction was rejected.

## Status

Still 'documented limitation, defer until triggered' — no implementation work scheduled. When triggered (a future scheduler that produces topology-divergent or name-divergent graphs), the implementation target is topology-equivalent comparison, not name resolution.

## Hard rules carry over

Implementation directives unchanged: Opus 4.7, no fallback paths, no parallel APIs.

comments.text:
## First implementation attempt rejected (2026-05-08)

Implementer's branch `worktree-agent-a5c0b52ccbc2cf5c5` (commit `f93608cc00`) cannot land. Two reasons:

1. **Edge key dropped positions entirely** — the literal spec called for positions IN the edge key. Implementer cited 22-test failure under the literal spec and chose to drop positions, citing the keep-Failures constraint. But the literal spec was satisfiable with a small classifier-pipeline branch in `diagnose_missing_edge` (return [] when both endpoints exist with no order inversion). That's a pipeline tweak, NOT a Failure-hierarchy change, so it's permissible under keep-Failures.

2. **More fundamentally: the implementation does NOT achieve register-allocation invariance.** The implementer used `_byte_keys_for_resource` outputs (which produce absolute physical-register byte-keys like `('v', 8)`, `('v', 12)`) as the edge key's byte_offset component. Two graphs with the SAME topology but DIFFERENT register allocations produce DIFFERENT byte-keys → different identities → no match. This defeats wic4's whole reason for needing wx9.3.

The memo's spec `(src_role, src_position, sink_role, sink_position, edge_kind, byte_offset)` meant **intra-operand byte position** (e.g., 0..3 for a 4-vgpr LR's outputs flowing to consumer inputs), NOT absolute physical-register byte-key. This was ambiguous in the memo — fixing the wording.

Cleaned up the rejected worktree. Re-dispatching with corrected spec.

title: Phantom-edge fix: Pack scratch-vgpr reuse in _resolve_producers
description:
# The problem

Pack instructions reuse a small pool of scratch vgprs (e.g., v133)
across PackA0 and PackB0 chains. The current _resolve_producers in
ScheduleCapture.py yields every writer of a register whose lp <
consumer_lp - it doesn't pick the latest one. So when PackB0[3] reads
v133, the resolver builds edges to ALL prior writers of v133 (PackA0's
earlier write, PackB0's earlier write, etc.) instead of just the most
recent one.

# Symptom

On real TF32 captures this generates ~24,688 false-positive cross-side
OrderInverted failures.

# Why this is hard

The right answer is \"newest writer in stream order whose value the
consumer actually receives.\" In hardware terms: skip writers whose
result has been overwritten before the read. Multiple
newest-writer-in-stream-order attempts were tried during sub-task
11/12 work and reverted because the simple stream-order resolver broke
18 unrelated tests - the wait/quad-cycle conditions for \"is this
writer's value still live\" are non-trivial:

- SWait drain for memory ops
- Quad-cycle gap for MFMA
- Immediate visibility for ALU

User direction during the prior attempts: \"better to have the newest
writer be added regardless of condition for the purpose of
construction, and then have the conditions be verified in a second
pass where we return the failure case.\" That two-pass design (add
newest writer optimistically; verify hardware visibility separately)
is the most promising direction explored so far but was not finished.

# Hard constraint from prior conversation

The compare_graphs(default, cms) production assertion at
KernelWriter.py:5178 stays. User: \"We will not remove it, that would
mean that we miss non swait related bugs. never suggest again.\"
Phantom edges must be eliminated by fixing the resolver, not by
weakening the assertion.

# Why it matters

Holds back re-enabling _GenericALURule for the P1 Pack/VSwap/VCC
register gaps documented in test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py.
Sub-task 11's cross-iter OrderInverted gate (commit f594ff4b09)
handles cross-iter Pack -> MFMA correctly, but cross-side
within-iter Pack reuse still triggers phantom edges.

# Status

Active design problem. No agreed approach. Independent of sub-task 12
(coordinate-system change does not fix the resolver's many-writers
behavior).

# Investigation suggestions

- Reproduce on the TF32 capture that produced the 24,688 failures to
  re-confirm current behavior.
- Re-attempt the two-pass design: pass 1 yields the latest writer in
  stream order regardless of condition; pass 2 walks the resulting
  edges and emits a typed Failure when the writer's value isn't
  actually visible to the consumer.
- Check whether MFMA acc handling from sub-task 10 (MFMA acc tracking
  via WrappedInstruction) gives any reusable machinery for tracking
  liveness.
close_reason: completed

title: Sub-B: Pass 1 — per-byte latest-writer construction in _resolve_producers
description:
# Goal

Replace the current _resolve_producers cross-product (yields every prior overlapping writer) with a forward sweep that yields exactly ONE edge per (consumer, distinct latest writer) pair. Hardware-visibility checks deferred to Sub-C.

# Algorithm

Replace Phase 2 of build_dataflow_graph (ScheduleCapture.py:2258-2314) with:

1. Build a flat list of all dataflow nodes sorted by _logical_position.
2. Initialize latest_writer: dict[byte_key, (writer_node, overlap_resource)].
3. Walk nodes in ascending _logical_position. For each node:
   - For each read_resource in wrapper.reads: enumerate byte_keys, look up latest_writer, group by writer to merge contiguous bytes back into a single overlap container, emit ONE DataflowEdge per distinct writer with merged_overlap.
   - For each write_resource in wrapper.writes: enumerate byte_keys, OVERWRITE latest_writer[byte_key] with this writer (older writers forgotten).

# Per-byte map design (option a from design doc)

byte_key shape:
- Numeric vgpr/sgpr: (regType, regIdx)
- Symbolic: (regType, regName.name, offset)
- m0: (regType, 0)
- LDS / MemoryRegion: (regType, range_start_byte) per byte

This preserves the multi-writer-narrow-write invariant TestMultiWriteProducer (test_dataflow_graph_builder.py:597-694) currently asserts — different bytes resolve to different writers, so two narrow writes feeding one wide read still yield two edges.

# Cross-iter scoping (critical)

latest_writer must be keyed (byte_key, consumer_iter_or_lower) so iter-N+1 Pack writes don't shadow iter-N writes for an iter-N consumer. Concretely: when looking up byte_key for consumer at iter K, find the writer with iter <= K that is latest in stream order. Implementation: maintain per-iter latest_writer maps and look up by walking iters K..0.

# Tie-breaking

Two writers at same _logical_position for same byte: raise CaptureConsistencyError (matches existing posture at ScheduleCapture.py:43-79). The _intra_seq tiebreak (wx9.1 will replace with sub_index) makes this near-impossible.

# Files touched

- Tensile/Components/ScheduleCapture.py — replace _resolve_producers (1690), restructure build_dataflow_graph Phase 2 (2258-2314), introduce _byte_keys_for_resource(resource) helper. Keep _intersection / _reg_intersection unchanged.
- Fix the docstring lie at ScheduleCapture.py:2161-2163 (currently claims "latest in LOGICAL ORDER" but doesn't deliver — Sub-B makes it true).

# Verification

- pytest Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_builder.py — TestEdgeRegisterIntersection, TestMultiWriteProducer (semantics may change — see note), TestMFMASelfRAW.test_mfma_acc_chain_reorder all pass.
- Sub-A's regression test (test_dataflow_graph_phantom_edges.py) flips from XFAIL → PASS; remove xfail marker.
- TestMultiWriteProducer note: if its assertion was "yield two edges from two writes feeding one wide read", per-byte map preserves that. If it was "yield two edges from two distinct writes to the SAME bytes by the SAME producer", that becomes "one edge with merged overlap" — semantic update needed; document the change in the test.

# Estimated LoC

~150 lines (helper ~40, rewritten resolver ~70, build_dataflow_graph adjustments ~40).

# Depends on

Sub-A (rocm-libraries-wx9.4.1) — need the failing fixture before flipping it.

title: Sub-C: Pass 2 — per-(producer-category, consumer-category) visibility dispatch
description:
# Goal

After Sub-B's per-byte latest-writer Pass 1 emits one edge per (consumer, distinct writer), Pass 2 verifies hardware-level visibility per edge and emits typed Failures when the writer's value is NOT actually visible.

# Visibility rules table (per consumer category)

| Consumer | Resource | Visibility requirement | Failure on miss |
|---|---|---|---|
| DSLoad LR* reading vgpr LDS-addr | vgpr | immediate (ALU) | OrderInvertedFailure (same-iter only) |
| DSLoad LR* reading LDS bytes | MemoryRegion | lgkmcnt drain since LW/LWS | MissingWaitFailure / WaitOnWrongCounterFailure / WaitInsufficientFailure |
| BufferLoad GR* reading vgpr (vaddr) | vgpr | immediate | OrderInvertedFailure |
| BufferLoad GR* reading sgpr (SRD) | sgpr | immediate | OrderInvertedFailure |
| BufferLoad GR* reading m0 (DTL) | mgpr | immediate | OrderInvertedFailure |
| MFMA reading vgpr a/b | vgpr | immediate (ALU writer) OR quad-cycle gap (MFMA writer) | OrderInvertedFailure / TimingTooCloseFailure |
| MFMA reading vgpr accumulator | vgpr | quad-cycle gap of N | TimingTooCloseFailure |
| Consumer reading from BufferLoad (vmcnt path) | vgpr | vlcnt drain since the load | MissingWaitFailure family |
| Pack/scalar ALU consumer | vgpr/sgpr | immediate | OrderInvertedFailure |

# Key change

Drop the MFMA-as-producer wait-coverage exemption at ScheduleCapture.py:2620-2621 and 2891-2894. Replace with quad-cycle gap check.

# Quad-cycle gap N

Constants exist at CMSValidator.py:275-282:
- QUAD_CYCLES_STANDARD_MFMA_FINISH = 3
- QUAD_CYCLES_MFMA_4X4_FINISH = 1
- QUAD_CYCLES_CVT_BEFORE_MFMA = 2
- QUAD_CYCLES_MFMA_4X4_BEFORE_CVT1 = 5

For MFMA→MFMA acc-RAW: producer's mfma_finish_cycles (3 standard, 1 for MFMAPack).

# Open question (validate during coding)

Does precompute_issue_times (CMSValidator.py:2646) need to be exposed/imported, or does the existing estimated_quad_cycles_before_result_used plumbing on Pack (CMSValidator.py:388) suffice? Prefer keeping ScheduleCapture import-free of CMSValidator (would create import cycle). Likely re-implement _quad_cycle_gap_ok(producer, consumer, num_mfma_per_iter) locally using stream position deltas.

# Failure types — reuse

All five rules map to existing Failure types at ScheduleCapture.py:478-762 (OrderInvertedFailure, MissingWait family, TimingTooCloseFailure, MissingBarrierFailure). NO new Failure subclass.

# Files touched

- Tensile/Components/ScheduleCapture.py — diagnose_missing_edge (2567-2720), validate_edge_wait_coverage / _classify_edge_coverage (2839-2960). Add _quad_cycle_gap_ok helper. Per-(producer, consumer) dispatch table.

# Verification

- All existing test_dataflow_graph_*.py tests pass.
- New unit test asserts MFMA acc-chain emits TimingTooCloseFailure when gap < N (was silent pass before).
- Production assertion at KernelWriter.py:5202 does NOT fire on the TF32 corpus (gfx950/custom_mainloop_scheduling_tf32.yaml, custom_xfp32.yaml).

# Estimated LoC

~100 lines.

title: Sub-D: Re-enable _GenericALURule for Pack/VSwap/VCC P1 register gaps
description:
# Goal

Add _GenericALURule to the operand registry (_OPERAND_RULES at ScheduleCapture.py:1908-1915) so Pack/VSwap/scalar-ALU instructions publish wrapper.reads/wrapper.writes. This is the downstream goal that the phantom-edge fix unblocks — once Sub-B/C eliminate phantoms, the ALU rule can run without flooding the comparison with false positives.

# Rule shape

class _GenericALURule:
    @classmethod
    def applies(cls, inst):
        # Catch-all for vgpr/sgpr ALU instructions not handled by earlier rules.
        # Earlier rules (DSLoad, DSStore, DTL, BufferLoad, MFMA, NoDataflow) win.
        return _is_alu_instruction(inst)
    
    def reads_writes(self, inst):
        params = inst.getParams()
        writes = (params[0],) if _is_register(params[0]) else ()
        reads = tuple(p for p in params[1:] if _is_register(p))
        return reads, writes

Order matters in _OPERAND_RULES — _GenericALURule MUST come last (after _NoDataflowRule absorbs SWait/SBarrier/SNop, after MFMA/DSLoad/etc claim their classes).

# Tests that should flip from XFAIL → PASS

In Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py:

title: Canonical-reference refactor: comparisons against default schedule, kill kind_rank
description:
# Why this exists

Today _logical_position embeds kind_rank — a hardcoded table at ScheduleCapture.py:1589-1620 mapping category bases (LR*, LW*, GR*, Pack*, MFMA) to integer ranks (0-6). The tuple (body, iter, kind_rank, intra_seq) is used to:

1. Sort producers in the resolver via producers_by_kind buckets (ScheduleCapture.py:2270-2287).
2. Classify OrderInverted by comparing positions WITHIN a single graph (ScheduleCapture.py:2599-2610, 2886-2888).
3. Encode a "canonical pipeline order" (LR -> LW -> GR -> Pack -> MFMA) used as the implicit reference for "did CMS reorder this?".

This is structurally wrong. ALL cross-schedule comparisons should reference the default schedule's actual emit order, not a synthetic hardcoded order. The default schedule IS the canonical order by definition.

# Pathologies kind_rank causes

- PackA + PackB share rank 5 -> the producers_by_kind bucket aliases cross-side, producing the phantom-edge bug tracked in wx9.4.
- GRA + GRB + GR + GRIncA + GRIncB share rank 4 -> same bucket-aliasing class for global reads.
- The intra_seq tiebreaker (capture-time _graph_nodes offset) IS schedule-dependent, so the "schedule-invariant lp" claim is already false.
- Hardcoded mapping doesn't generalize - new categories must be retrofitted (currently 16 entries, raises if missing at line 1683).

# Target design

- compare_graphs reads default[node].position (SchedulePosition: loop_index, vmfma_index, sub_index) as the canonical reference for ordering.
- OrderInverted means: "in default, producer.position < consumer.position; in subj, producer.position > consumer.position" (or relative-order disagrees in any way).
- _logical_position collapses to a stream-order key (body_idx, vmfma_index, sub_index) - or is deleted entirely if compare_graphs takes over the ordering responsibility.
- _KIND_RANK, _MFMA_KIND_RANK, intra_seq, _intra_seq, _split_category_iter (pieces of it) all delete.
- Resolver Pass 1 (wx9.4.2 Sub-B) walks in stream order (vmfma_index, sub_index) - cleaner than walking in lp order.

# Subtasks

- 9.5.1: Refactor compare_graphs OrderInverted to use default-schedule reference
- 9.5.2: Audit and migrate other "expected order" callsites (same-iter gates, _node_iter, _MFMARule deferral)
- 9.5.3: Delete _KIND_RANK / _MFMA_KIND_RANK / intra_seq machinery; collapse _logical_position

# Subsumes

- rocm-libraries-wx9.1 (Sub-task 12: intra_seq -> sub_index): made moot by 9.5.3 since intra_seq is deleted entirely.

# Sequencing

This epic is a prerequisite for wx9.4.2 (Sub-B). Sub-B's per-byte latest-writer algorithm wants to walk in stream order; if we do this epic first, Sub-B is cleaner. wx9.4.1 (Sub-A regression fixture) is independent and can proceed in parallel.

# Verification

Full unit suite stays green throughout each subtask. End-to-end TF32 build (gfx950/custom_mainloop_scheduling_tf32.yaml, custom_xfp32.yaml) confirms no behavioral regressions in OrderInverted detection.

title: Sub 9.6.1: Refactor compare_graphs OrderInverted to consult default-capture positions
description:
# Goal

Replace the within-graph lp-comparison in OrderInverted classification with a cross-graph comparison against the default capture's actual stream order.

# Current behavior (problems)

ScheduleCapture.py:2599-2610 and ScheduleCapture.py:2886-2888 classify OrderInverted by comparing producer.lp vs. consumer.lp WITHIN the subj graph. lp encodes a synthetic canonical order via kind_rank — meaning "OrderInverted" actually means "CMS deviates from the LR -> Pack -> MFMA pipeline assumption baked into _KIND_RANK".

This is wrong. The default schedule IS the canonical order. If default emits Pack-then-MFMA and CMS emits the same way, that's not an inversion — even if some other schedule would have done LR-then-Pack-then-MFMA. Conversely, if default emits Pack-A then Pack-B then MFMA and CMS emits MFMA before Pack-B, that IS an inversion regardless of what kind_rank says.

# New design

OrderInverted detection becomes a cross-graph operation in compare_graphs (ScheduleCapture.py:2490-2564):

1. For each edge (producer, consumer) found in default graph, look up the same producer/consumer identities in subj graph.
2. Compare default[producer].position vs default[consumer].position (canonical: producer should be earlier).
3. Compare subj[producer].position vs subj[consumer].position.
4. If the relative order disagrees -> emit OrderInvertedFailure with both positions for diagnostics.

Use SchedulePosition lexicographic comparison (loop_index, vmfma_index, sub_index) — already implemented at ScheduleCapture.py:321-343 with @functools.total_ordering.

# Files touched

- Tensile/Components/ScheduleCapture.py — diagnose_missing_edge (2567-2720), _classify_edge_coverage (2839-2960). Replace lp-based gates with default-position lookups. Threading: compare_graphs already has both graphs in scope, but the diagnose/classify helpers may need plumbing for default-graph access.
- OrderInvertedFailure (definition near line ~580): may need to grow `default_producer_position` / `default_consumer_position` fields for diagnostics.

# Verification

- All existing test_dataflow_graph_comparison.py / test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py tests pass. Some OrderInverted-asserting tests may need fixture updates if they relied on kind_rank's specific bucket ordering.
- New test: cross-side Pack reorder (PackA0 -> MFMA0, PackB0 -> MFMA0) where default emits PackA-PackB-MFMA and subj emits PackB-PackA-MFMA. With the new logic this is NOT an OrderInverted (both ALU writes complete before MFMA reads, immediate visibility). With old kind_rank logic it might or might not flag — depends on intra_seq.

# LoC estimate

~80-120 lines.

# No dependency

Can start immediately. Subsequent 9.6.2 / 9.6.3 build on this.

6. CMSValidator.py side: any "expected ordering" assumptions in verify_correct_number_of_instructions, verify_ascending_order, verify_scc_overlap. ## Sites confirmed schedule-invariant (no migration needed)

### _node_iter (ScheduleCapture.py:1637-1650)

Hardware fact: MFMA latency is governed by issue-timing constraints, not the dscnt/vlcnt FIFO model. NOT a canonical-order assumption. Sub-C (wx9.4.3) replaces with quad-cycle gap check; that's a hardware refinement, not a default-reference migration. **Stays.**

### producers_by_kind sort (ScheduleCapture.py:2270-2287)
Primary kind_rank consumer. Replaced by per-byte latest-writer map in Sub-B (wx9.4.2).

Used by _resolve_producers + producers_by_kind. After Sub-B, becomes dead. Deleted in wx9.6.3.

### CMSValidator.py:409, 414, 529 — three OrderInvertedFailure emitters

These come from `Pack.validate()` and `GlobalRead._validate_must_start_after()`. They compare `self.issued_at` against constraint-derived positions (`must_start_after.done_idx()`, `needed_by.issued_at`). The constraints come from the validator's own structural analysis of the (single) schedule under test — the validator has no default reference.

These emit `OrderInvertedFailure` for a conceptually-distinct event: "an instruction violates a declared dependency constraint", as opposed to the cross-graph `compare_graphs` event "subject reverses default's relative order".

**Two options:**
- **Option A**: keep reusing `OrderInvertedFailure`. The default_*_position fields stay optional forever. Document in the dataclass docstring that these are populated only by the cross-graph classifier.

### CMSValidator structural rules (verify_ascending_order, verify_scc_overlap)
These check correctness invariants on the captured schedule itself (non-decreasing vmfmaIndices for grouped instructions, no SCC clobbers between SCC-coupled groups). These are hardware/correctness rules, not order comparisons against any reference. **Stays.**

title: Rebuild DTL m0 test fixture: make_gr produces non-DTL _FakeGR
description:
## Failing tests (xfail strict=True)

- `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py::TestDTLm0Tracking::test_dtl_m0_update_before_buffer_load` (line 175-203)
- `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py::TestDTLm0Tracking::test_dtl_m0_add_update_before_buffer_load` (line 205-234)

## Root cause

Both tests build their BufferLoad consumer via `dataflow_fixtures.make_gr(...)` (defined at `Tensile/Tests/unit/dataflow_fixtures.py:178-191`). `make_gr` constructs a `_FakeGR` with a non-None vgpr `dst` field. Inside `ScheduleCapture._is_dtl_buffer_load` (line 1770-1781) the DTL signal is `_inst_dst(inst) is None`. With a vgpr dst, `_BufferLoadRule` claims the instruction (line 1837-1846) and publishes `reads=(srd,) writes=(dst,)` — no m0 read.

The m0 setter (real `SMovB32` / `SAddU32`) IS correctly handled by `_GenericALURule`: `writes=(mgpr(0),) reads=(sgpr(LWA),...)`. But because no instruction in the fixture reads m0, no edge ever forms between the m0 setter and the BufferLoad → `compare_graphs` returns `[]`.

Confirmed via `pytest --runxfail` (excerpt):
```
g_subj = build_dataflow_graph(_wrap(subj_cap))
failures = compare_graphs(g_ref, g_subj)
assert failures   # AssertionError: assert []
```

## Fix sketch

Add a `make_dtl_buffer_load(...)` helper to `dataflow_fixtures.py` (or extend `make_gr` with a `dtl=True` kwarg) that builds a real `rocisa.instruction.BufferLoadB128` with `MUBUFModifiers(lds=True)` and `dst=None` — the same shape used by the already-passing `TestWrappedInstructionPopulation::test_dtl_rule_contributes_m0_read` (file lines 260-267). Then update both `TestDTLm0Tracking` tests to use the new helper and drop the `@pytest.mark.xfail`.

## Verify

After fix: `pytest Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py::TestDTLm0Tracking -v` should show both tests passing without `--runxfail`. Suite total should move from 623p/5xf to 625p/3xf.

## Production impact

None. The production `_DTLBufferLoadRule` correctly publishes m0 as a read for real DTL BufferLoads (covered green by `test_dtl_rule_contributes_m0_read`). This is purely test-fixture coverage.

title: Model VSwap symmetric R+W in _GenericALURule
description:
## Failing test (xfail strict=True)

`Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py::TestVSwapPair::test_vswap_pair_reorder_invisible` (line 533-559)

## Root cause — both fixture-blind AND a real semantic gap

`VSwapB32(dst, src)` swaps the two operands: BOTH registers are read AND written. `_GenericALURule.extract` (`Tensile/Components/ScheduleCapture.py:1924-1933`) treats it asymmetrically:

```
writes = (params[0],) iff is_register
reads  = tuple(p for p in params[1:] if is_register)
```

So `VSwapB32(v0, v1)` yields `writes=(v0,) reads=(v1,)`. For the test:

- ref: `sw1=Swap(v0,v1)` then `sw2=Swap(v1,v2)`. sw1 writes v0/reads v1; sw2 writes v1/reads v2. **No edge between sw1 and sw2** under the asymmetric model (they share v1 but as sw1.read + sw2.write, not RAW/WAR).
- subj: sw2 then sw1. Now sw2.write(v1) → sw1.read(v1) creates a RAW edge in SUBJECT.

`compare_graphs` only flags edges present in REF but missing from SUBJ (`Tensile/Components/ScheduleCapture.py:2575-2577`: `missing_keys = ref_keys - subj_keys`). The reorder forms a NEW edge in SUBJ — invisible.

This is a real semantic gap: a correct VSwap model would publish `reads = (params[0], params[1])` AND `writes = (params[0], params[1])`. With that, the ref order has the dependency (sw1.write(v0) preceding sw2.read of nothing on v0; but v1 is sw1.read+write→sw2.read+write — WAW edge sw1→sw2 exists in REF).

Confirmed via `pytest --runxfail`: `compare_graphs(g_ref, g_subj) == []`.

## Fix sketch

Two layered options (combine both for full coverage):

1. **VSwap-specific rule** in `_OPERAND_RULES` (insert before `_GenericALURule`):
   ```python
   class _VSwapRule:
       def applies(self, inst, _):
           return type(inst).__name__ in {'VSwapB32', 'VSwapB16'}
       def extract(self, inst, _):
           p = list(inst.getParams())
           regs = tuple(x for x in p[:2] if _is_register(x))
           return regs, regs   # both R and both W
   ```
2. (Optional) Generalize: any `compare_graphs` could ALSO flag SUBJECT-only edges as `OrderInvertedFailure` (bidirectional). But that's a wider design change with cross-side false-positive risk — see related VCC bead.

## Production impact

VSwap is currently used in CMS-emitted Pack code paths (PackA0/PackB0). The dataflow graph is silently missing one edge class. No known production miscompiles — Pack scheduling has plenty of other constraints — but it removes a safety net.

## Verify

After fix: `pytest Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py::TestVSwapPair -v` passes without `--runxfail`.
close_reason: completed

title: Track VCC as a resource (or rebuild VAddCO/VAddCCO test fixture)
description:
## Failing test (xfail strict=True)

`Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py::TestVCCCarryChain::test_vcc_carry_chain_reorder` (line 573-605)

## Root cause — TWO independent issues

### Issue 1: VCC is opaque to the resolver

`rocisa.container.VCC` instances expose `regType=None, regIdx=None` (verified via inspection script). `_is_register` (`Tensile/Components/ScheduleCapture.py:1784-1789`) requires both attributes to be non-None, so VCC is filtered out of every rule's reads/writes. The carry-out of `VAddCOU32` and the carry-in of `VAddCCOU32` are therefore invisible to the dataflow graph — the entire purpose of the chain.

### Issue 2: Test fixture's vgpr-WAW claim is wrong

The test's docstring asserts: 'the vgpr WAW is wrong even ignoring VCC.' This is false. With `lo=VAddCOU32(dst=v100, ..., src0=v100, src1=v50)` and `hi=VAddCCOU32(dst=v101, ..., src0=v101, src1=v51, src2=VCC)`, the two instructions touch DISJOINT vgprs (lo: v100,v50; hi: v101,v51). So even with proper symmetric tracking, no edge exists in REF between lo and hi via vgprs — only via VCC.

Plus the same one-directional `compare_graphs` issue as in wx9.8 (VSwap): if the only edge ever forms in subject, it's invisible.

Confirmed via `pytest --runxfail`: `compare_graphs == []`.

## Fix sketch — pick one (or both)

### Option A: Track VCC as a synthetic resource

Extend `_is_register` (or add a dedicated `_is_resource`) to recognize `type(x).__name__ == 'VCC'` as a tracked operand, with a synthetic resource key like `('vcc', 0, 1)` so the per-byte resolver can hash it. Then `VAddCOU32` writes vcc, `VAddCCOU32` reads vcc → RAW edge in REF that's missing in SUBJ (where the order is swapped).

Risk: any operand named VCC across the build would now contribute to dataflow tracking — audit `extract` callers in `_OPERAND_RULES` for unexpected VCC params (e.g. `VCmp*` writes VCC implicitly via destination — those would need a class-specific rule too).

### Option B: Rebuild the fixture to make the failure detectable today

If VCC tracking is out of scope for the next sprint, change the fixture so `hi` actually reads a vgpr that `lo` writes (e.g. `hi.src1 = vgpr(100, 1)` to make hi consume lo's dst). Then the existing `_GenericALURule` produces a RAW edge in REF that's missing in SUBJ → test passes. The test's documentation should be updated to clarify it's exercising 'vgpr chain through VAddCCOU32', not VCC tracking.

## Production impact

Real CMS-emitted carry-add chains (`globalReadIncrement` non-buffer path, `KernelWriterAssembly.py:9120-9146`) currently have no dataflow protection on their VCC dependency. Reorders would break the 64-bit add. No known production miscompiles, but the existing wait-cnt scheduling appears to be the only safety net.

## Verify

After fix: `pytest Tensile/Tests/unit/test_dataflow_graph_register_gaps.py::TestVCCCarryChain -v` passes without `--runxfail`.
close_reason: completed

title: Discuss the NodeLike Union pattern between graph-side and structural-side validation

  - Graph-side (the dataflow comparison pipeline): cms_node_label receives a GraphNode that has body_label, tagged_inst, and a position computed from SchedulePosition.
  - Structural-side (per-instruction validate() overrides on GlobalRead and SWait, e.g. CMSValidator.py:3123 and :3216): the override has a ValidatorInstruction in hand, not a GraphNode. It still wants to construct failure labels in the same wording (so that MissingWaitFailure / MissingBarrierFailure look identical regardless of source path).

The Union exists because both callers reuse cms_node_label, and the helper discriminates with getattr probes (category exists on both -- as a property on one, a field on the other).

User wants to discuss in more detail. Topics likely to come up:
  - Is the Union the right abstraction, or should ValidatorInstruction grow a to_node_label() method (or a thin GraphNode wrapper) so cms_node_label only handles one shape?
  - The structural-side path passes body_capture=None, which forces the bare-category fallback in cms_node_label. Is the loss-of-precision (no [N] suffix) acceptable, or should the structural side carry enough body context to compute the index?
  - Are there more callers of cms_node_label that will inherit the Union vs. one-shape question?
  - Does the eventual codegen-vs-codegen (rocm-libraries-5gd) generalization simplify or complicate the Union?

Discussion only -- no behavior change without user direction.

**Carry-forward from rocm-libraries-hdem (2026-05-12):** the hdem implementation substituted the literal byte-key tuple from ORAM1 §4.1 with `(producer.identity, consumer.identity, ...)` because the byte-key tuple lost producer-discrimination in two scenarios (`swap_pack` differently-classed-on-same-byte; cross-iter `LR_first`/`LR_second` same-class-same-byte). If two captures render the SAME physical write differently — e.g., one symbolically as `v[vgprValuA_X0_I0:...+3]` and one numerically as `v[40:43]` because one resolved through `name_to_idx` and the other did not — identity-tuples DIVERGE while byte-keys would have MATCHED. Future migration to byte-key matching (or a hybrid: identity-first, fall back to byte-key on render-divergence) is feasible without re-plumbing edge formation.

title: Add integration test exercising mfmaReorder end-to-end through graph-native validator
description:
## Discovered by

Follow-up question during c44-bead-cleanup: "Do we have any tests that verify mfmaReorder is handled correctly?"

## Current coverage state

The graph-native unit suite has two test classes that *simulate* mfmaReorder by manually placing MFMAs at "reordered" slot indices:

- `TestLRBeforeMFMA_MfmaReorder` in `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_validate_lr_before_mfma_graph.py:473`
  - `test_reordered_MFMA_at_late_slot_with_covering_swait` (positive)
  - `test_reordered_MFMA_at_early_slot_swait_too_late` (negative)

- `TestLRBeforeMFMA_ForceUnrollSubIter` in the same file (sibling case for slot permutations)

These verify the graph-native rule is INVARIANT under MFMA reordering: the validator reads register operands directly, so reordered MFMAs still form the same LR -> MFMA edges. The class docstring at lines 461-470 documents this design.

## The gap

**No test passes a real `mfmaReorder=[...]` array end-to-end.** The full production path looks like:

1. `ScheduleInfo(..., mfmaReorder=[0,1,2,3, 8,9,10,11, ...])` constructs an opt-schedule with explicit reordering.
2. `CustomSchedule.expand_macro` (CustomSchedule.py:336-337) applies the permutation: `mfmaCode = [mfmaCode[x] for x in opt1.mfmaReorder]`.
3. `MAINLOOP` macro emits the reordered MFMAs into the captured stream.
4. `build_dataflow_graph` builds the graph from the (already-reordered) capture.
5. `compare_graphs` + `validate_edge_wait_coverage` validate it.

Steps 1-3 are exercised by real-kernel captures (the production path), but no UNIT test pins that the end-to-end pipeline handles a mfmaReorder permutation correctly. If a future change to `expand_macro`'s permutation logic or `build_dataflow_graph`'s node-position assignment introduced a subtle bug, the unit suite wouldn't catch it.

## Lower-confidence existing coverage

`Tensile/Tests/unit/test_ScheduleCapture.py` has `TestRealKernelCapture` and similar classes that build captures from real kernel macros. SOME of those kernels MAY use `mfmaReorder`. Audit which ones — that's prerequisite work for this bead.

## Action

1. **Audit existing real-kernel captures.** Grep `test_ScheduleCapture.py` for kernels that pass mfmaReorder. Document which (if any) implicitly exercise the production path.

2. **If implicit coverage exists**: write a docstring comment in `TestLRBeforeMFMA_MfmaReorder` pointing at the implicit-coverage test, to make the existing setup self-documenting.

3. **If no implicit coverage exists**: add an explicit test that:
   - Constructs a `ScheduleInfo` with a non-trivial `mfmaReorder=[...]` array (e.g. `[0,1,2,3, 8,9,10,11, 4,5,6,7, 12,13,14,15]` — a real shape from CustomSchedule.py:1366).
   - Runs `expand_macro` to emit the reordered MFMA stream.
   - Builds the graph from the resulting capture.
   - Asserts validation passes (positive) and asserts a SPECIFIC induced ordering bug (e.g. an LR moved out of order with respect to the reordered MFMAs) fires `MissingWaitFailure` (negative).

4. Place in `test_ScheduleCapture.py` (where the production-path coverage lives) or a new `test_mfma_reorder_e2e.py` if the test is large enough to warrant its own file.

## Why P3

The graph-native rules are MFMA-position-invariant by design (verified by the existing two tests). A bug in production-path mfmaReorder handling would surface in real-kernel captures during CI; the missing unit test is defense-in-depth, not a load-bearing safety net.

## Related

- `c44` — verification bead that surfaced the question.
- `wao` — porting bead; classified `TestValidatePackTF32MFMAReorder` as REDUNDANT under the same "graph is reorder-invariant" reasoning.

title: Default-side KernelWriter capture pipeline double-captures pack-MFMA objects (mfma_index=-1, two sequence positions)
description:
## Symptom

Surfaced by 4up4 (rocm-libraries-4up4) implementation. The default-side `KernelWriter` capture pipeline emits the **same Python rocisa pack-MFMA object twice** with two different category tags (`PackA0` and `PackA3`) under `mfma_index=-1` at two different `slot.sequence` positions. The CMS-side capture emits it once.

## Concrete evidence (from 4up4 implementer)

For canonical TF32 4×4 TN production kernel:
- Object id `128298338355792` appears at `(PackA3, mfma_index=-1, sequence=4)` AND `(PackA3, mfma_index=-1, sequence=44)` in default's `ML` body.
- Same object appears once at `(PackA3, mfma_index=43, sequence=1)` in CMS's `ML` body.
- 12 such double-captures per body in `ML` and `ML-1` = **24 spurious extra default-side identities per build**.

## Why hidden until now

Under the historical identity tuple `(class_tag, loop_index, canonical_render)`, pack-MFMAs collapsed to `class_tag='PACK'` and `PACK` was excluded from `_DATA_FLOW_KINDS = ("LR", "LW", "GR", "MFMA")`. The 24 spurious identities never entered the data-flow set, so `compare_graphs` never saw the divergence.

Under 4up4's new identity tuple `(loop_index, canonical_render, emission_ordinal)` with rocisa-derived data-flow filter, pack-MFMAs (real `MFMAInstruction` rocisa class) are correctly classified as `InstructionCategory.MFMA` by `_category()` and enter the data-flow set. `compare_graphs`'s entry-time check at `CMSValidator.py:3306-3336` raises `CaptureConsistencyError` listing the 24 only-in-reference identities — exactly per design memo `EMISSION_ORDINAL_DESIGN.md` §2.7:

> "emit-count divergence IS a real defect, not something to absorb."

## Failing tests (gated by this bug, currently failing on 4up4 branch)

18 real-kernel tests across:
- `tensilelite/Tensile/Tests/unit/test_ScheduleCapture.py`
- `tensilelite/Tensile/Tests/unit/test_cms_from_default.py`
- `tensilelite/Tensile/Tests/unit/test_prologue_capture.py`
- `tensilelite/Tensile/Tests/unit/test_cross_subiter_alu_carveout_real_kernel.py`

Plus 3 xfailed regression tests in `test_dataflow_graph_emission_ordinal.py` that should flip to passing once this fix lands.

## Investigation needed

The implementer-agent identified the symptom but did NOT trace the code path producing the double-capture. Investigation must answer:

1. **Where in `KernelWriter` is the same Python pack-MFMA object appended twice to the default-side capture's slot list?** Trace through `_loopBody` and `_noLoadLoopBodyDefault` (or whatever code path produces the default-side capture).
2. **Is it a category-tagging bug** (same object recategorized twice with different category tags) **or a slot-list double-append** (same object literally appended twice to the slot list)?
3. **What's the principled fix?** Per user's standing rules: no tactical patches that perpetuate CMS coupling, no "cheap pragmatic" framing. If the fix has architectural choices, STOP and surface them.

## Sequencing

- **Blocks rocm-libraries-4up4 merge** to `users/alvasile/validator_long_term_plans`. 4up4's implementation is complete on its agent worktree branch but cannot land while 18 unit tests fail on top of it.
- **Independently valuable**: this is a real bug regardless of how identity is constructed. Fix can land on the validation branch directly.

## References

- `Tensile/Components/EMISSION_ORDINAL_DESIGN.md` §2.7, §2.8 (the design that surfaced this).
- 4up4 implementation: 3 commits on agent worktree branch `worktree-agent-a4185c2af90971c4a` (in `/home/alvasile/rocm-libraries/.claude/worktrees/agent-a4185c2af90971c4a`).
- `Tensile/Components/CMSValidator.py:3306-3336` (the `CaptureConsistencyError` raise that surfaces this).
close_reason: Superseded by F3 (rocm-libraries-vybd, commit 03ca4ef0d30). The same-id leftover-pack double-capture defect is resolved by deleting the leftover-pack walk entirely. The X-fix work on worktree-agent-ae1362302b95bff89 is discarded; F3's same-id invariant test (TestNoDoubleCaptureUnit in test_capture_pipeline_checks.py) provides the regression pin.

title: 5gd.A.2: Implement cms_capture_to_timeline() bridge
description:
## Parent: 5gd Part A — input-shape refactor

Implement `cms_capture_to_timeline(capture: ScheduleCapture) -> Timeline`. The bridge from the existing CMS shape into the source-agnostic Timeline.

## Concrete tasks

1. Walk the four bodies (ML-1, ML, NGL, NLL) of a `ScheduleCapture` in execution order.
2. For each scheduled instruction, build a `TimelineEvent` carrying:
   - position (loop_index, vmfma_index, sub_index — preserved as-is for now).
   - `tagged_inst` = the existing CMS category label (`LRA0[12]`, etc.).
   - register reads/writes (already in the CMS metadata).
   - body label.
3. Verify the timeline can be fed into the existing graph builder without behavior change.
4. Pin the equivalence: `validate(capture)` and `validate(cms_capture_to_timeline(capture))` produce identical results across the test suite.

## Done when

- Helper exists and is unit-tested.
- Equivalence test passes for every existing CMS fixture.
